genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a member of staff lives on the lowest floor of the building, beside the entrance door
his duties fall into three separate groups
the first group covers the cleanliness of the shared areas
he puts a lubricant on the closing mechanisms that squeak
the second group concerns the delivery of letters
he carries the post to the door of the oldest residents
the third group consists of calming quarrels between neighbours
he hears the sides in conflict one after the other
he does not pass on what he learns about the residents' lives
he nearly always finds the owner of a lost object
text: The caretaker lives on the lowest floor of the building, in a flat wedged against the front door. Everything he does falls into three separate groups. The first is cleaning: he sweeps the stairwell, wipes down the glass panes in the entrance hall and oils the latches that have begun to squeak. The second is the post, which he sorts through at the start of each week and leaves outside the doors of the oldest tenants. The third is peacekeeping. When two neighbours fall out, he hears each of them on their own, then suggests something both can live with. What people trust most is his silence, for he knows everyone's habits and repeats none of them. They value his memory for lost property too. A key, a glove, an umbrella left behind in the lift nearly always finds its way back to its owner.

units: the piece of furniture reviewed was bought second-hand
on arrival its surface was covered with a sticky layer the seller had not mentioned
this old coating had to be stripped off entirely
the supports of the piece began to wobble the following week
simply tightening them put this fault right without taking the whole thing apart
after a season of use the overall verdict is favourable
the material stands up to very hot containers
one drawer jams when the air turns damp
no adjustment cures this jamming
the piece is judged worthwhile given its low cost
text: This coffee table came to us second-hand, and a season of steady use has settled the question. It turned up looking dull, the top hidden under a sticky varnish that the seller had said nothing about, so the whole surface had to be stripped back before anything else could be done. A week later the legs began to wobble; tightening the screws sorted that out, with no need to take the thing apart. After a season of family use, the verdict leans firmly the right way. The wood takes a scalding mug without marking, scratches rub out with a cloth, and the height suits reading as well as eating in front of a screen. One fault remains. The drawer jams whenever the air turns damp, and no amount of adjusting cures it. For what it cost, it earns its place, provided that nuisance is accepted.

units: the kitchen refurbishment has just been finished
a workman uncovered a cracked pipe behind the sink
the seeping had been going on for several weeks
the damp made the wall covering crumble at a touch
the leak had to be sealed before any finishing work
the water supply had to be cut off during the repair
the washing-up was done at a neighbour's for five evenings
costs rose and the timescale stretched out
the writer invites her correspondent to come and see the room
text: I am writing because the kitchen is finally done, and you will never guess what held the whole job up. While digging away at the wall behind the sink, the workman came upon a pipe with a crack running through it. Water had been seeping for weeks, and the plaster crumbled the moment you laid a hand on it. The split had to be sealed before anyone could think about paint. Since the repair meant shutting off the water, we spent five evenings carrying the washing-up upstairs to the neighbour. She lent us her bowl, and we came back down with the plates still warm. The upshot: the budget swelled, the dates slipped, and my temper went with them. Now that everything has dried, the room smells of fresh paint and I sit in it for no reason at all, just to look at a smooth wall. Come and see it as soon as you can.

units: workshops open to everyone take in household appliances that no longer work
a workshop coordinator answers the visitors' questions
the main obstacle is not the scarcity of parts
owners give up because they believe the inside of an appliance is out of bounds
the method chosen is to have the visitor carry out the action
the visitor lifts the lid himself and cleans the clogged part
a helper steps in when the repair goes beyond the visitor's abilities
this help takes place in full view of the appliance's owner
more objects leave in working order than are left behind
text: What is to be done with a kettle that has given up? The question comes round again and again at the repair workshops that open their doors to all comers, and the woman who runs one of them is glad to answer it. The barrier, she explains, is not a shortage of spare parts but the discouragement of the owners themselves, who are convinced that a sealed casing is none of their business. How do you shift a belief like that? By handing over the job rather than describing it: the visitor lifts the lid himself, spots the clogged filter and rinses it under the tap. And when the fault outruns what he can manage? A helper takes over, though never out of sight of whoever brought the thing in, who follows every step. The measure of it is simple. Far more objects walk out working than are left behind.

units: a resident thought the countryside better than the noise of a block of flats
her neighbour had lived in both settings
the neighbour disputed this preference
she described the sounds of wood and wind in an isolated house
she said that no voice covers those sounds in the countryside
she liked recognising the residents' steps on the stairs
the first wanted a planted plot and warm water at the outside tap
the second told apart quiet, which one chooses, from the presence of others, which one takes in
the two women reached no agreement
they greeted each other the next day nonetheless
text: The tenant downstairs held that the hush of a country house beat the bustle of a block of flats. Her neighbour answered gently that she had lived in both and believed nothing of the sort. Out there, she said, the wind worries the shutters and the floorboards creak with no human voice to cover them; you end up listening to your own solitude. Here the stairs ring with familiar steps, and every step carries a face: the nurse coming home, the student going out, the child dragging a satchel. The first woman pressed her case. She wanted a garden of her own, the smell of cut grass, warm water running from the tap outside. The second smiled and said that quiet is something you choose, whereas company is something you take in. They parted still disagreeing, and greeted one another the next day.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before running water arrived, three techniques served to wash cloth
the first technique used water mixed with sifted ashes
this alkaline solution dissolved greasy substances
the second technique rested on blows struck with a wooden tool
the beaten cloth was then rinsed and left to drain on a hard surface
the third technique exposed the cloth spread out on damp vegetation
damp and sunlight together removed the stains
these processes damaged the fibres, whose weave turned coarse
the wear explains why cloth was counted, mended and handed down
text: Before water came into houses under pressure, the washing of linen rested on three methods that the old handbooks set out in careful detail. The first was a soak in ash water: the pieces were heaped in a tub and drenched with water thickened by sifted ashes, and the dissolved potash bit into everything greasy. The second came down to brute force. A wooden beater drove the fibres against a sloping board, after which they were rinsed and left to drain on a flat stone. The third turned on sunlight; spread over wet grass, the cloth gave up its stains to damp and daylight working together. All three of them wore the weave down, and after a dozen washes the surface felt coarse under the fingers. That wear is why household cloth was counted, mended and handed on as something of value.

units: the observation concerns a kitchen window during a cold night
preparing food releases steam into the room
this damp air meets a pane chilled from outside
the steam turns into droplets settling on the glass
the droplets merge then run down the panel
the water gathers against the horizontal piece of wood, which soaks it up
at dawn the condensation goes from the glass surface
the wood stays soaked with water despite this disappearance
the repetition of the phenomenon lifts the paint and encourages fungus
airing the room briefly after cooking stops the process at its very start
text: Watch what happens to a kitchen window over one cold night. Early in the evening, cooking sends up steam and the air of the room fills with a damp you cannot see. By the end of the meal that warm air reaches the pane, which the cold outside has chilled. The steam gives up its energy and turns back to liquid, so a fine beading settles across the glass. Later on the neighbouring beads run together, grow heavier and slide down towards the bottom of the frame. There they gather against the wooden crosspiece, which drinks in part of the water. Come dawn the mist has gone from the surface, yet the wood underneath stays soaked. Repeat that cycle through a whole season and the paint lifts and fungus takes hold. Open a window briefly after cooking and the chain breaks at its first link.

units: a bicycle was left against railings after a move
repeated rain attacked the transmission, which seized up
the workshop in the area quoted a wait of two weeks
the owner therefore took on the repair unaided
he cleaned every link with a solvent and a stiff brush
the noise of the work drew a neighbour carrying tools
the neighbour straightened the back wheel, which had play in it
this mutual help gave rise to a weekly meeting
the two men mend the objects left behind in the building
the bin store no longer holds any wrecks
text: The bicycle had been propped against the railings since the end of summer, forgotten in the rush of a move. One shower after another had eaten into the chain until the links would not turn at all. The workshop down the road quoted a wait of two weeks, so its owner set about the job on his own. He laid the frame down on a sheet, poured solvent over the metal and worked at every single link with a stiff brush. The old grease, gone tacky, came away in flakes. The scraping brought down a neighbour with an oilcan and a spanner. The back wheel had picked up some play for want of the right tool, and the man had it running true in a handful of movements. Out of that favour grew a habit: once a week the pair mend what the building gives up on, and the bin store has emptied of wrecks.

units: a door gives out a shrill noise every time it is moved
the procedure avoids calling in a tradesman
you must first find the guilty hinge by moving the door slowly
a cloth placed underneath protects the floor from drips
you use a thin oil and not a thick paste
a thick paste picks up dirt and makes matters worse
a single drop placed on the pin is enough
swinging the door several times spreads the product
you wipe off the surplus once it has run down
if the noise carries on, the upper fixing of the hinge must be tightened
text: Does your door shriek every time someone goes through, and wake you at night? Here is how to be rid of it without paying anyone. Start by tracking down the guilty hinge: ease the door open very slowly indeed and listen for where the squeal begins. Then slip a cloth underneath, because whatever runs down will mark the floor. Reach for a thin oil, never a thick grease: grease holds the dust and the trouble comes back worse than before. One drop on the pin will do. Swing the door back and forth a dozen times so the oil works its way down. Let it drain, then wipe the surplus away with the cloth. If the squeal hangs on, the top screw has probably worked loose; tighten it right home, or the door will keep leaning crookedly on its hinges. Quiet returns before the evening is out.

units: two neighbouring districts have adopted opposite strategies to revive their shops
on the high bank, a covered market was built with public money
the pitches there are offered at low rent to growers from round about
this market's attendance reaches its peak as the week ends
on the lower bank, no building received funding
local people grouped together and use an old school yard
every seller sets up a folding stand of his own there
the covered market attracts passing buyers drawn by steady opening hours
the yard keeps a nearby clientele who put up with bad weather
in both districts, the shops in the surrounding streets receive more visitors
text: Two neighbouring districts have taken opposite routes to bring their local shops back to life, and the contrast is hard to miss. On the high bank a covered market went up with public money; pitches go cheaply to growers from round about, and the crowds peak as the week ends. On the low bank not a brick was funded. The residents there banded together instead and took over the yard of an old school, where every trader brings a folding table of his own. The takings differ as much as the settings. The covered hall pulls in passing custom, won over by the shelter and by fixed opening hours, while the yard keeps a nearby following that puts up with rain and improvisation. One thing joins the two experiments. In both, the shops in the streets round about have seen more people through the door.
